newsitem.title: USA: NYC Hevesi says won improvements to watershed pact.
newsitem.headline: NYC Hevesi says won improvements to watershed pact.

text.p: New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi said Tuesday he had won major improvements to the $2.2 billion watershed agreement between the city, the state and upstate communities, but he warned questions remain.
The pact aims to protect the city's drinking water while avoiding the high costs of filtering it.

The improvements include a much stronger program to monitor how the agreement is implemented, and an analysis of the scientific basis of the deal to ensure changes can be made to protect water quality, Hevesi said in prepared remarks.
The National Academy of Sciences is expected to do an independent study of the pact and analyze how best to protect the city's water.

"New York City must continue to have clean, safe, low-cost and good-tasting water. Right now, we cannot be sure if this agreement will accomplish those goals," said Hevesi, in prepared remarks, explaining the study was crucial because it would tell the city how to fix any problems.

As a result of the improvements, Hevesi, who was not involved in the watershed negotiations and who said he saw "serious weaknesses" in the first pact, agreed to settle suits involving the city and registered contracts, clearing the way for the city to begin implementing it.
The agreement calls for the city to negotiate land purchases from communities that surround its resevoirs to protect the areas from development.

Flaws in the first pact, which was trumpeted last autumn when it was reached by New York Gov. George Pataki and New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, included no limit on how many new sewage treatment plants could pump water into the city's resevoirs, the transfer of millions of dollars to upstate communities without adequate checks, and a "lopsided partnership" with the city facing big penalities for not paying upstaters while they not face any if they did not uphold their side of the bargain, Hevesi said.

Also, the state would have been transferred the primary enforcement responsibility by the federal Environmental Protection Agency, even though its oversight was needed because it was not involved in upstate-downstate fights over water, Hevesi said. Further, there would not have been an early opportunity to modify the program if the city's water quality declined, he added.
